q: An organization runs virtual machines in a public cloud IaaS environment. Under the shared responsibility model, who is responsible for patching the guest operating systems?
opts: The customer
The cloud provider
The hypervisor vendor
The internet service provider
exp: In IaaS the provider secures the physical facility, hardware, and hypervisor, while the customer owns the guest OS, applications, configuration, and data. The provider patches only what it controls; hardware vendors and ISPs have no role in guest patching.
tip: Rule of thumb: IaaS = customer owns most; PaaS = customer owns app and data; SaaS = customer owns data, identity, and configuration.

q: A company adopts a SaaS CRM platform. Which security responsibility ALWAYS remains with the customer?
opts: Managing user identities, access rights, and data classification within the application
Patching the application servers
Securing the physical data center
Maintaining the platform's underlying database engine
exp: Identity, access management, and the data itself never transfer to the provider. Application patching, facility security, and database engine maintenance are provider responsibilities in SaaS.
tip: You can outsource operations, never accountability. Data and identity remain yours in every service model.

q: A defense contractor must ensure a classified research network has no network path to any other network. Which architecture provides this?
opts: Physical isolation with an air gap
Logical segmentation with VLANs
Software-defined networking with microsegmentation
A jump server with MFA
exp: An air gap physically separates networks so no routed path exists. VLANs and SDN provide logical separation that shares physical infrastructure and can be misconfigured or bypassed. A jump server still constitutes a connection between zones.
tip: Air gap trade-offs: strongest isolation but painful updates and data transfer, plus removable-media risk.

q: Which benefit does software-defined networking provide that traditional per-device configuration does not?
opts: Centralized, programmatic control of forwarding policy across many devices
Elimination of the need for any physical switches
Automatic encryption of all traffic by default
Guaranteed immunity to denial-of-service attacks
exp: SDN separates the control plane from the data plane and manages policy centrally through APIs, enabling rapid, consistent change. Physical switches still forward traffic, encryption must be configured explicitly, and SDN does not prevent denial of service.
tip: SDN security note: the controller becomes a high-value target and a single point of failure — protect and monitor it heavily.

q: A cloud team defines all network and server configuration in version-controlled templates deployed through a pipeline. Which security benefit does this MOST directly provide?
opts: Consistent, reviewable, and repeatable configurations that reduce drift and misconfiguration
Automatic detection of zero-day vulnerabilities
Elimination of the need for identity and access management
Guaranteed compliance with all regulations
exp: Infrastructure as code makes configuration auditable, peer-reviewable, and reproducible, which reduces the misconfigurations that dominate cloud incidents. It does not detect unknown vulnerabilities, replace IAM, or produce regulatory compliance on its own.
tip: IaC risk to remember: a mistake or an embedded secret propagates instantly to every environment. Scan templates and secrets in CI.

q: Which statement about serverless (function as a service) architecture is accurate from a security standpoint?
opts: The provider manages the runtime and OS, so customer focus shifts to code security, permissions, and secrets management
Serverless functions cannot be exploited because they are short-lived
Serverless removes the need for logging and monitoring
The customer must patch the underlying operating system
exp: Serverless removes OS management from the customer but concentrates risk in application code, over-permissive execution roles, dependency vulnerabilities, and secret handling. Short lifetimes reduce persistence but not exploitation, monitoring remains critical, and OS patching is the provider's job.
tip: Serverless pitfalls: excessive IAM permissions on the function role, injection through event data, and vulnerable dependencies.

q: A monolithic application is refactored into 40 microservices communicating over HTTP APIs. Which new security concern becomes MOST significant?
opts: A large increase in east-west service-to-service traffic requiring authentication, authorization, and encryption between services
Loss of the ability to use TLS
Inability to log application events
Mandatory use of a single shared database credential
exp: Decomposition multiplies internal API calls, so each service boundary needs mutual authentication, authorization, and encryption — commonly delivered by a service mesh. TLS remains available, logging is still possible (and more important), and shared credentials are an antipattern rather than a requirement.
tip: Microservices security keywords: mTLS, service mesh, API gateway, per-service identity, and least-privilege service accounts.

q: Which statement correctly compares containers to virtual machines?
opts: Containers share the host kernel, so isolation is weaker than VMs but startup and density are better
Containers each run a full guest operating system, making them heavier than VMs
Containers cannot be scanned for vulnerabilities
Containers provide stronger isolation than hardware-assisted virtualization
exp: Containers virtualize at the OS level and share the host kernel, giving efficiency at the cost of a weaker isolation boundary; a kernel vulnerability can affect all containers on the host. VMs include full guest operating systems, container images are routinely scanned, and hypervisor isolation is stronger.
tip: Container hardening: minimal base images, no root, read-only filesystems, image signing, registry scanning, and runtime policy.

q: A water treatment facility's SCADA systems cannot tolerate downtime and run protocols with no built-in authentication. Which architectural approach is MOST appropriate?
opts: Segment the OT network from IT, allow only brokered one-way or tightly filtered flows, and monitor passively
Place SCADA devices on the corporate VLAN so existing controls apply
Enable automatic operating system updates on all controllers
Expose the historian to the internet for vendor support
exp: Operational technology requires strict IT/OT segmentation with controlled data brokering (such as a DMZ with a data diode or unidirectional gateway) and passive monitoring that will not disturb fragile devices. Flat placement with IT, aggressive automatic patching, and internet exposure all raise risk of outage or compromise.
tip: OT priorities invert IT's: availability and safety first, then integrity, then confidentiality.

q: Which characteristic of a real-time operating system creates the greatest security constraint?
opts: Deterministic timing requirements make patching and heavyweight security agents difficult to introduce
RTOS platforms cannot use any form of encryption
RTOS devices always have unlimited compute resources
RTOS software is immune to buffer overflows
exp: Real-time systems must meet strict timing guarantees, so updates and resource-hungry agents may be unacceptable, pushing protection to the network and physical layers. Encryption is possible but constrained, resources are typically limited, and RTOS code is written in memory-unsafe languages just like other embedded software.
tip: Embedded and RTOS mitigations: network isolation, secure boot, signed firmware, and vendor-supported update processes.

q: A company deploys 500 IP cameras with default credentials and no update mechanism. Which mitigation should be implemented FIRST?
opts: Place the cameras on a dedicated segmented VLAN with no internet access and change all default credentials
Enable UPnP so the cameras can configure their own firewall rules
Assign each camera a public IP address for easier management
Rely on the vendor's cloud portal for security
exp: Segmentation plus credential remediation immediately reduces both exposure and the most likely compromise path. UPnP automatically opens inbound access, public IPs increase exposure, and relying on a vendor portal delegates control without reducing local risk.
tip: IoT playbook: isolate, change defaults, disable UPnP/unneeded services, restrict egress, and monitor for anomalous traffic.

q: Which trade-off BEST describes a centralized security architecture compared to a decentralized one?
opts: Consistent policy and simpler oversight, but the central component becomes a single point of failure and a high-value target
Lower consistency but automatic redundancy for every function
No need for change management because control is unified
Improved resilience because all decisions occur in one place
exp: Centralization brings uniform policy, easier auditing, and economies of scale, at the cost of concentrated failure and attack impact. Decentralization improves independence and blast-radius containment but complicates consistency. Change management is always required.
tip: Whenever an architecture centralizes control, expect an exam answer about single point of failure and protecting the control plane.

q: By moving email to a managed cloud provider with contractual security obligations and purchasing cyber insurance, an organization is primarily practicing which architectural consideration?
opts: Risk transference
Risk avoidance
Risk acceptance
Attack surface elimination
exp: Shifting some consequences and obligations to another party through contracts and insurance is risk transference. Avoidance would mean not using email at all, acceptance means absorbing the risk without action, and outsourcing does not eliminate the attack surface.
tip: Insurance and contracts transfer financial impact, not accountability. Regulators still hold the data owner responsible.

q: Which security challenge is MOST characteristic of hybrid cloud environments?
opts: Maintaining consistent identity, policy, and visibility across on-premises and cloud platforms with different control sets
The impossibility of encrypting data in transit between environments
Complete loss of on-premises logging capability
A regulatory prohibition on hybrid architectures
exp: Hybrid designs must reconcile differing native controls, identity systems, and telemetry formats, which creates gaps and inconsistent enforcement. Encryption between environments is standard practice, on-premises logging continues, and hybrid architectures are not prohibited.
tip: Hybrid answers usually involve federated identity, unified logging into one SIEM, and consistent policy as code.

q: An architecture review flags a proprietary appliance whose vendor issues firmware updates only once per year and does not publish vulnerability details. Which consideration does this represent?
opts: Limited patch availability increasing exposure duration
Excessive compute requirements
Insufficient power redundancy
Lack of data sovereignty
exp: Slow or unavailable patches lengthen the window during which known flaws remain exploitable, requiring compensating controls. Compute, power, and sovereignty are separate architectural considerations.
tip: SY0-701 lists both 'patch availability' and 'inability to patch' as architecture considerations — expect them as answer choices.

q: Administrators must manage servers in a protected zone without exposing management ports to the user network. Which appliance is designed for this?
opts: Jump server (bastion host)
Load balancer
Web application firewall
Reverse DNS resolver
exp: A jump server is a hardened, heavily monitored single entry point for administrative access into a protected zone. Load balancers distribute traffic, WAFs inspect HTTP requests, and DNS resolvers translate names.
tip: Harden jump servers aggressively: MFA, session recording, no internet access, minimal software, and strict inbound source restrictions.

q: A network security appliance is configured to block all traffic if its inspection engine crashes. Which failure mode is this, and what is the primary trade-off?
opts: Fail-closed; security is preserved but availability may be lost
Fail-open; availability is preserved but traffic goes uninspected
Fail-safe; both security and availability are guaranteed
Fail-secure; the device automatically reboots into a bypass mode
exp: Fail-closed (fail-secure) denies traffic on failure, protecting security at the expense of availability. Fail-open permits traffic uninspected, protecting availability at the expense of security. No mode guarantees both.
tip: Life-safety systems (door egress) typically fail-open for human safety; data security devices usually fail-closed.

q: A team wants to monitor traffic for threats with zero risk of introducing latency or an outage. Which deployment should they choose?
opts: Passive monitoring via a network tap or SPAN port
Inline intrusion prevention in blocking mode
A transparent proxy in the traffic path
A layer 7 firewall performing TLS interception
exp: A tap or SPAN copies traffic out of band, so the sensor cannot affect the production path. Inline IPS, transparent proxies, and intercepting firewalls all sit in the path and can introduce latency or failure.
tip: Passive/tap = detect only, no impact. Inline = can block, but becomes a potential point of failure.

q: Which control is specifically designed to inspect and filter HTTP/HTTPS requests for attacks such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting?
opts: Web application firewall
Stateful packet-filtering firewall
Network load balancer
Network access control appliance
exp: A WAF understands HTTP semantics and can block application-layer attack patterns. A stateful firewall filters by addresses, ports, and connection state. A load balancer distributes requests, and NAC governs which devices may join the network.
tip: WAF operates at layer 7 for web apps. It is a compensating control, not a substitute for secure coding.

q: Which capability distinguishes a next-generation firewall from a traditional layer 4 stateful firewall?
opts: Application awareness and user identity-based policy with integrated deep packet inspection
The ability to perform network address translation
Support for static routing
The ability to log denied packets
exp: NGFWs identify applications regardless of port, tie policy to user identity, and inspect payloads, often adding IPS and TLS inspection. NAT, routing, and logging are present in traditional firewalls as well.
tip: Layer 4 firewall = ports and IPs. Layer 7/NGFW = applications, users, and content. UTM = many functions bundled in one appliance.

q: An organization wants to inspect and filter employee web browsing, cache content, and hide internal addresses from external sites. Which device provides these functions?
opts: Forward proxy server
Reverse proxy server
Layer 2 switch
DHCP server
exp: A forward proxy sits between internal clients and the internet to filter, log, cache, and mask client addresses. A reverse proxy fronts servers to protect and distribute inbound requests. Switches forward frames, and DHCP assigns addresses.
tip: Forward proxy protects and controls clients going out. Reverse proxy protects servers receiving traffic in.

q: Which device improves both availability and scalability by distributing client requests across multiple backend servers and removing failed nodes from rotation?
opts: Load balancer
Jump server
Intrusion detection sensor
Network tap
exp: Load balancers spread traffic using scheduling algorithms and perform health checks to bypass failed servers. Jump servers broker administrative access, IDS sensors detect threats, and taps copy traffic for monitoring.
tip: Know the modes: active/active uses all nodes for capacity; active/passive holds a standby node for failover.

q: A company must ensure that any device plugging into a conference room network jack is authenticated before receiving network access. Which technology should be implemented?
opts: 802.1X port-based network access control with EAP
DHCP reservations for known devices
MAC address filtering on the access switch
A captive portal on the wireless controller
exp: 802.1X authenticates the supplicant at the port before granting access, typically using EAP methods against a RADIUS server. DHCP reservations do not restrict access, MAC filtering is easily spoofed, and captive portals apply after network attachment and are typically wireless.
tip: 802.1X components: supplicant, authenticator, authentication server. Strongest EAP method on the exam is EAP-TLS with certificates.

q: Which EAP method provides mutual certificate-based authentication of both client and server and is considered the most secure option for enterprise wireless?
opts: EAP-TLS
EAP-MD5
PEAP with MSCHAPv2 only
LEAP
exp: EAP-TLS requires certificates on both ends, eliminating password-based attacks. EAP-MD5 offers no mutual authentication and is obsolete, PEAP-MSCHAPv2 protects passwords inside a TLS tunnel but still relies on credentials, and LEAP is a deprecated proprietary method vulnerable to offline cracking.
tip: If certificates are mentioned as available, EAP-TLS is the expected answer.

q: Which IPsec component provides confidentiality, and which provides only integrity and authentication?
opts: ESP provides confidentiality plus integrity; AH provides integrity and authentication without encryption
AH provides confidentiality; ESP provides integrity only
IKE provides confidentiality; ESP provides key exchange
Both AH and ESP provide identical services
exp: Encapsulating Security Payload encrypts and authenticates the payload, while Authentication Header authenticates without encrypting. IKE negotiates keys and security associations rather than protecting payloads directly.
tip: Also know tunnel mode (encrypts the entire original packet, used site-to-site) versus transport mode (protects the payload only).

q: A remote user's laptop is configured so that only traffic destined for corporate subnets goes through the VPN while internet browsing goes directly out. Which configuration is this, and what is the main security concern?
opts: Split tunneling; the endpoint bypasses corporate inspection for internet traffic
Full tunneling; all traffic is inspected but bandwidth is consumed
Site-to-site tunneling; branch traffic is aggregated
Transport mode IPsec; only payloads are protected
exp: Split tunneling reduces VPN load and improves performance but removes corporate visibility and filtering from internet-bound traffic, creating a potential bridge between the internet and the corporate network. Full tunneling routes everything through the corporate egress, and the other options describe different deployment concepts.
tip: Split tunnel = performance, less inspection. Full tunnel = inspection and control, more bandwidth and latency.

q: A distributed workforce needs consistent security policy and low-latency access to cloud applications without backhauling all traffic to headquarters. Which architecture BEST fits?
opts: Secure access service edge combining SD-WAN with cloud-delivered security services
A single on-premises UTM appliance at headquarters
Site-to-site IPsec tunnels from every home office to the data center
A dial-up remote access server pool
exp: SASE delivers networking and security (SWG, CASB, ZTNA, FWaaS) from cloud points of presence near the user, eliminating hairpin routing while keeping policy consistent. A single appliance and universal backhaul create latency and a bottleneck, and dial-up is obsolete.
tip: SASE = SD-WAN + cloud security stack. ZTNA is the access component that replaces broad VPN network access.

q: Where should an internet-facing web server that must also query an internal database be placed?
opts: In a screened subnet (DMZ), with tightly restricted rules permitting only required database traffic inward
On the internal LAN with a public IP assigned directly
On the same subnet as domain controllers for performance
Outside the firewall with no filtering to simplify troubleshooting
exp: A screened subnet isolates internet-facing services so a compromise does not directly expose internal systems, while narrow rules permit only the necessary backend flow. The other placements collapse security zones or remove protection entirely.
tip: Zone design principle: public-facing services in the DMZ, data tier internal, and only explicitly required flows between them.

q: An IDS sensor is deployed to detect attacks against internet-facing services before they reach internal networks. Where is the MOST effective placement?
opts: Monitoring traffic at the network perimeter between the internet edge and the screened subnet
On the guest wireless VLAN only
Inside a single application server's loopback interface
On an isolated lab network with no production traffic
exp: Sensors must see the traffic of interest, so perimeter placement covers inbound attacks against exposed services. Guest VLANs, loopback interfaces, and lab networks do not carry the relevant traffic.
tip: Sensor placement rule: visibility follows traffic. Decide what you must see, then place the sensor where that traffic flows.

q: Which switch feature prevents an attacker from connecting a rogue switch that floods the CAM table to force the switch into fail-open flooding behavior?
opts: Port security limiting the number of learned MAC addresses per port
Enabling Spanning Tree Protocol only
Setting a static IP address on the switch
Increasing the switch's MTU
exp: Port security caps MAC addresses per port and can shut down or restrict violating ports, defeating MAC flooding. STP prevents loops rather than table exhaustion, and IP or MTU settings are unrelated.
tip: Switch attacks and defenses: MAC flooding → port security; ARP poisoning → DAI; rogue DHCP → DHCP snooping; STP manipulation → BPDU guard.

q: Which design provides the HIGHEST availability for a critical customer-facing application?
opts: Active/active clustering across two geographically separate regions with automated failover and health-based traffic steering
A single high-specification server with a redundant power supply
Nightly backups to an offsite vault
A warm standby server restored manually within eight hours
exp: Geographic active/active clustering with automated failover eliminates single points of failure at both the server and site level. Redundant power protects one component, backups enable recovery rather than continuous availability, and a manually restored warm standby produces hours of downtime.
tip: Availability ladder: single server < redundant components < local cluster < multi-site active/passive < multi-region active/active.

q: Which firewall rule design principle should be applied at the end of every access control list?
opts: An explicit deny-all rule with logging
An explicit allow-all rule for troubleshooting
A rule permitting ICMP from any source
A rule allowing all outbound traffic on any port
exp: An explicit final deny with logging enforces default-deny posture and creates evidence of blocked attempts. Broad allow rules, unrestricted ICMP, and unrestricted egress undermine control and enable exfiltration and reconnaissance.
tip: Rule order matters: most specific first, implicit deny last, and always log denies. Also filter egress, not just ingress.

q: An organization deploys TLS interception at the perimeter. Which concern MUST be addressed for this to work without breaking client trust?
opts: The inspection appliance's issuing CA certificate must be trusted by managed endpoints, and exemptions are needed for pinned or sensitive traffic
TLS interception requires disabling all certificate validation on clients
Interception eliminates the need for endpoint protection
Interception works only with TLS 1.0
exp: Interception re-signs traffic with an internal CA, so endpoints must trust that CA, and categories such as banking, health, and certificate-pinned applications typically require bypass. Disabling validation would be dangerous, endpoint protection remains necessary, and modern TLS versions are supported.
tip: TLS inspection trade-offs: visibility versus privacy, performance cost, and breakage of pinned applications.

q: Which appliance is used to aggregate and normalize telemetry from many sources to support detection and investigation?
opts: A SIEM platform collecting logs and events from sensors and devices
A layer 2 access switch
A DHCP relay agent
A network time server
exp: SIEM platforms aggregate, normalize, and correlate telemetry for alerting and investigation. Switches forward frames, DHCP relays forward address requests, and time servers synchronize clocks — though accurate time is a prerequisite for correlation.
tip: Accurate NTP is a hidden exam favorite: without synchronized time, log correlation and forensics fall apart.

q: What is the PRIMARY security-relevant benefit of a deliberate multi-cloud strategy?
opts: Reduced dependence on a single provider, limiting the impact of one provider's outage or compromise
Elimination of the shared responsibility model
A single native control plane for all environments
Automatic regulatory compliance in every jurisdiction
exp: Multi-cloud reduces concentration risk and vendor lock-in, improving resilience. It does not remove shared responsibility, and it actually complicates control-plane consistency and compliance rather than simplifying them.
tip: Platform diversity and multi-cloud both address correlated failure — the trade-off is operational complexity and skills cost.

q: A company must prevent unmanaged personal devices from accessing internal applications while allowing corporate laptops. Which combination is MOST effective?
opts: Device certificate-based authentication with posture assessment through conditional access policies
A shared VPN password distributed to employees
Blocking access from non-corporate IP addresses only
Requiring users to promise not to use personal devices
exp: Device identity plus posture checks distinguish managed from unmanaged endpoints regardless of network location. Shared passwords do not identify devices, IP-based restrictions fail for remote work and can be circumvented, and honor-system policy is unenforceable.
tip: Modern access control decision inputs: user identity, device identity, device health, location, and risk signals.

q: Which architectural characteristic BEST describes the ability to add capacity quickly in response to demand without redesigning the system?
opts: Scalability
Resilience
Risk transference
Data sovereignty
exp: Scalability is the capacity to grow (or shrink) to meet demand. Resilience is the ability to withstand and recover from failure, risk transference shifts consequences to another party, and data sovereignty concerns legal jurisdiction over data.
tip: Scalability = handle more load. Elasticity = scale up and down automatically. Resilience = survive failure.

q: Which approach follows Zero Trust principles more closely than a traditional full-network VPN for third-party contractor access?
opts: Zero trust network access granting per-application access after continuous verification
A site-to-site IPsec tunnel to the contractor's office network
A shared remote desktop account with a strong password
Opening RDP to the contractor's static public IP address
exp: ZTNA brokers access to specific applications rather than placing the contractor on the network, and it re-evaluates trust continuously. Site-to-site tunnels extend broad network trust, shared accounts destroy attribution, and exposed RDP is a well-known attack vector even when IP-restricted.
tip: Third-party access answers: per-application access, individual accounts, MFA, time-bound, session recording, and least privilege.

q: Which factor MOST often argues for keeping a workload on premises rather than migrating it to public cloud?
opts: Regulatory or contractual requirements that constrain data location and physical control
A desire to reduce capital expenditure
The need for rapid elastic scaling
A preference for provider-managed patching
exp: Data residency, sovereignty, and physical control requirements are common drivers for on-premises retention. Lower capital expenditure, elasticity, and managed patching are all arguments in favor of cloud adoption.
tip: Cloud pushes cost from capex to opex and adds elasticity; on-premises retains physical control and predictable latency.

q: A small branch office needs firewalling, antivirus, content filtering, and VPN termination in one cost-effective device. Which product category fits?
opts: Unified threat management appliance
Dedicated hardware security module
Layer 2 unmanaged switch
Passive network tap
exp: UTM consolidates multiple security functions into a single appliance, which suits small sites with limited budget and staff. HSMs manage cryptographic keys, unmanaged switches provide no security features, and taps only copy traffic.
tip: UTM trade-off: convenience and lower cost versus a single point of failure and possible performance limits when all features are enabled.

q: Which practice reduces the risk of unmanaged virtual machine sprawl?
opts: Enforce lifecycle policies with automated inventory, ownership tagging, and expiration of unused instances
Allow any developer to create VMs without approval to improve agility
Disable logging on non-production VMs
Use identical local administrator passwords across all VMs for consistency
exp: Lifecycle governance with inventory, ownership, and expiration prevents forgotten, unpatched systems from accumulating. Unrestricted creation causes sprawl, disabling logs removes visibility, and shared local admin passwords enable lateral movement.
tip: VM sprawl creates shadow assets: unpatched, unmonitored, and often forgotten in the asset inventory.

q: Which statement correctly distinguishes an IDS from an IPS in a network deployment?
opts: An IDS detects and alerts, typically out of band; an IPS sits inline and can drop malicious traffic
An IDS blocks traffic while an IPS only logs it
Both must be deployed inline to function
An IPS cannot generate alerts
exp: Detection systems observe and alert, while prevention systems are inline and can block. An IPS also generates alerts, and IDS deployments are commonly passive via tap or SPAN.
tip: False positives on an IDS create noise; false positives on an IPS create outages. That difference drives deployment decisions.

q: A security team must detect malicious activity in encrypted east-west traffic between application servers without decrypting it. Which approach is MOST practical?
opts: Deploy host-based sensors and EDR agents on the servers themselves
Add a second perimeter firewall
Block all encrypted traffic between servers
Rely solely on NetFlow volume totals
exp: Host-based visibility sees activity after decryption on the endpoint, which solves the encrypted-traffic blind spot. Perimeter devices do not observe east-west flows, blocking encryption is unacceptable, and flow volume alone gives limited detection detail.
tip: Encrypted traffic blind spots are addressed by endpoint telemetry, TLS inspection where feasible, or metadata analysis such as JA3 fingerprinting.

q: An architecture uses a single large database instance that all microservices depend on. Which resilience weakness does this create?
opts: A single point of failure whose loss disables every dependent service
Excessive geographic dispersion
Insufficient logging capability
Unavoidable data sovereignty violations
exp: Shared critical dependencies concentrate failure impact, negating much of the isolation benefit of microservices. Dispersion, logging, and sovereignty are not consequences of a shared database instance.
tip: Look for hidden single points of failure: shared databases, one authentication provider, one DNS resolver, or one internet circuit.

q: A hospital must keep medical imaging devices, guest Wi-Fi, and clinical workstations from communicating with each other. Which implementation BEST accomplishes this?
opts: Separate VLANs per zone with inter-VLAN traffic filtered by explicit firewall rules
One flat VLAN with host-based firewalls only
Assigning different DHCP scopes in the same broadcast domain
Using unique hostnames per device category
exp: VLANs paired with enforced filtering between them create real separation. Host-based firewalls in a flat network can be misconfigured or bypassed, separate DHCP scopes in one broadcast domain still permit direct communication, and naming conventions provide no isolation.
tip: VLANs alone only separate broadcast domains — segmentation requires filtering at the routed boundary.

q: Which protocol pairing correctly matches a secure alternative to its insecure counterpart?
opts: SNMPv3 replaces SNMPv1/v2c for encrypted, authenticated device management
TFTP replaces SFTP for secure file transfer
HTTP replaces HTTPS for secure web browsing
Telnet replaces SSH for encrypted administration
exp: SNMPv3 adds authentication and encryption that earlier versions lack. The other pairings are reversed: SFTP, HTTPS, and SSH are the secure options.
tip: Port pairs worth memorizing: 22 SSH/SFTP, 443 HTTPS, 465/587 SMTPS/submission, 636 LDAPS, 989/990 FTPS, 161/162 SNMP.

q: Which characteristic of embedded systems most complicates traditional vulnerability management?
opts: Long deployment lifecycles with limited or vendor-controlled update mechanisms
Standardized support for endpoint detection and response agents
Frequent, automatic security patches from multiple sources
Unlimited storage for security logs
exp: Embedded devices often remain in service for a decade or more with infrequent, vendor-gated firmware updates and no capacity for security agents. Broad EDR support, frequent patching, and generous logging are precisely what these devices lack.
tip: Compensate for unpatchable devices with network isolation, strict egress control, and passive monitoring.

q: A branch office has a single ISP circuit and loses all connectivity during a fiber cut. Which architectural change addresses this?
opts: Add a diverse secondary circuit from a different provider with automatic failover
Increase the bandwidth of the existing circuit
Add a second firewall behind the existing one
Enable quality of service on the router
exp: Provider and path diversity removes the single point of failure in connectivity. More bandwidth, added inline devices, and traffic prioritization do nothing when the only circuit is severed.
tip: Redundancy must be diverse to count: different provider, different physical path, and ideally different media.

q: An application must be protected against injection attacks, but the vendor cannot modify the code for six months. Which control provides the BEST interim protection?
opts: A web application firewall with tuned rules in blocking mode
A network intrusion detection sensor in passive mode
Increased password complexity for application users
More frequent database backups
exp: A WAF can block injection payloads at layer 7 as a compensating control while code remediation is pending. Passive detection does not prevent exploitation, password rules do not affect injection, and backups aid recovery rather than prevention.
tip: 'Cannot change the code yet' = compensating control, usually a WAF or virtual patch, with a documented remediation date.

q: Which architectural consideration is MOST relevant when deploying security agents to battery-powered field sensors?
opts: Limited power and compute budgets may make full agents impractical
Data sovereignty rules for sensor telemetry
The need for active/active clustering on each sensor
Requirements for TLS interception on the device
exp: Constrained power and processing capacity are the defining limits of field and IoT devices, which is why lightweight or network-based controls are used instead. Sovereignty, clustering, and interception are not the primary constraint in this scenario.
tip: SY0-701 explicitly lists power and compute among architecture considerations — remember them for IoT, embedded, and RTOS questions.
